group.title: Advanced phrasal verbs
group.tagline: Iron out, bank on, gloss over
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To solve small problems or difficulties.
examples: We need to {iron out} a few issues before the launch.
wrong: They ironed out the problems by making them much worse.

words.meaning: To depend on something happening or on someone doing something.
examples: Don’t {bank on} getting a refund.
wrong: I banked on his help, so I never expected him to come.

words.meaning: To avoid talking about a problem by treating it as unimportant.
examples: The report {glossed over} the safety failures.
wrong: She glossed over the mistake by explaining it in full detail.

words.meaning: To plan something carefully and in detail.
examples: We {mapped out} the project’s main stages.
wrong: They mapped out the trip by setting off with no plan.

words.meaning: To have to deal with a difficult problem or opposition.
examples: The plan {came up against} strong local resistance.
wrong: We came up against no problems, so it was very hard.

words.meaning: To be in charge of a team, group or project.
examples: She will {head up} the new research unit.
wrong: He heads up the team, so he has no say in it.

words.meaning: To get support or interest by making an effort.
examples: They held a concert to {drum up} support for the charity.
wrong: She drummed up support by hiding the event from everyone.

words.meaning: To give help or support to something that would otherwise fail.
examples: Government loans {propped up} the failing airline.
wrong: The loans propped up the firm, so it collapsed at once.

words.meaning: To add more details to a plan or idea.
examples: Can you {flesh out} the proposal for Monday?
wrong: He fleshed out the plan by cutting it to one line.

words.meaning: To include something when you plan or calculate.
examples: Remember to {factor in} the cost of shipping.
wrong: She factored in the travel time by leaving it out of the plan.

words.meaning: To reach an agreement after long and difficult discussion.
examples: The unions {hammered out} a deal with management.
wrong: They hammered out a deal in two seconds without talking.

words.meaning: To explain something clearly and in detail.
examples: The contract {spells out} who pays for repairs.
wrong: He spelled out the rules by keeping them vague and secret.

words.meaning: To keep thinking or talking about something, often something unpleasant.
examples: Try not to {dwell on} your past mistakes.
wrong: She dwelled on the problem by forgetting it instantly.

words.meaning: To start working seriously and with effort.
examples: It’s time to {buckle down} and study for the finals.
wrong: He buckled down by lying on the sofa all week.

words.meaning: To study or read something very carefully.
examples: Lawyers {pored over} the contract for days.
wrong: She pored over the report by glancing at it for a second.

words.meaning: To control something more strictly, such as spending.
examples: The government must {rein in} public spending.
wrong: They reined in costs by spending far more than before.

words.meaning: To reduce the size or amount of something.
examples: We had to {scale back} our plans for the festival.
wrong: They scaled back the project by making it twice as big.

words.meaning: To support or strengthen something that is weak or failing.
examples: The bank cut rates to {shore up} the economy.
wrong: They shored up the old wall by knocking it down.

words.meaning: To find information or meaning with patience and care.
examples: The study {teases out} the causes of the decline.
wrong: She teased out the meaning by refusing to look at the text.

words.meaning: To talk to someone to find out what they think about something.
examples: I’ll {sound out} the team before we decide.
wrong: She sounded out her colleagues by not asking anyone.

words.meaning: To stop something bad from happening for a time.
examples: The loan {staved off} bankruptcy for another year.
wrong: The snack staved off hunger, so I was starving at once.

words.meaning: To make a plan or statement weaker or less forceful.
examples: The final law was {watered down} after protests.
wrong: They watered down the rules by making them far stricter.

words.meaning: To be caused by something or come from it.
examples: Her fear of dogs {stems from} a childhood bite.
wrong: The problem stems from nothing and has no cause.

words.meaning: To mention a subject briefly.
examples: The lecture only {touched on} the history of the city.
wrong: He touched on the topic by talking about it for hours.

words.meaning: To reduce something gradually in size or number.
examples: We {whittled down} the list to three candidates.
wrong: They whittled down the list by adding fifty names.

words.meaning: To spend time in a relaxed way, often while waiting.
examples: We {whiled away} the afternoon playing cards.
wrong: He whiled away the hours by rushing from task to task.

words.meaning: To relax after work or stress; also to bring something slowly to an end.
examples: I read a book to {wind down} before bed.
wrong: She wound down by drinking strong coffee and working harder.

words.meaning: To avoid doing something by being clever or dishonest.
examples: He always {wriggles out of} washing the dishes.
wrong: She wriggled out of the task by doing all of it herself.

words.meaning: To focus all your attention on one thing.
examples: The inquiry {zeroed in on} the missing funds.
wrong: They zeroed in on the problem by ignoring it.

words.meaning: To leave an activity or job, especially after a long time.
examples: The singer {bowed out} after a final concert.
wrong: He bowed out of politics and ran for office again the next day.

words.meaning: To give some money or help as part of a group.
examples: Everyone {chipped in} to buy her a gift.
wrong: We all chipped in, so nobody gave anything.

words.meaning: To produce large amounts of something quickly, often of low quality.
examples: The factory {churns out} thousands of toys a day.
wrong: The studio churns out one film every twenty years.

words.meaning: To defend yourself against an attack, question or rival.
examples: The minister {fended off} questions about the scandal.
wrong: She fended off the attack by letting it happen freely.

words.meaning: To think about something carefully for a period of time.
examples: Let me {mull over} your offer this weekend.
wrong: He mulled over the offer by deciding in a split second.

words.meaning: To develop or turn out in a particular way.
examples: Let’s see how things {pan out} before we decide.
wrong: The plan panned out, so nothing happened at all.

words.meaning: To decide not to use a good chance.
examples: I can’t {pass up} an offer like that.
wrong: She passed up the chance by accepting it at once.

words.meaning: To start doing something new in addition to your usual activities.
examples: The bakery {branched out} into catering.
wrong: They branched out by doing only what they had always done.

words.meaning: To make money or gain an advantage from a situation.
examples: Shops {cashed in on} the sudden heat wave.
wrong: They cashed in on the trend by losing money on it.

words.meaning: To pay money for something, especially unwillingly.
examples: We had to {fork out} for a new boiler.
wrong: He forked out for the car by paying nothing.

words.meaning: To admit that you have done something wrong.
examples: Nobody {owned up to} breaking the window.
wrong: He owned up to the mistake by denying everything.
